newsitem.title: USA: Florida tobacco pension divestiture turns on one vote.
newsitem.headline: Florida tobacco pension divestiture turns on one vote.

text.p: Florida's anti-tobacco governor is pressing the swing vote on the state's pension board to agree to dump nearly $900 million worth of cigarette stocks from a state employees pension fund.

Along with two other trustees, Gov. Lawton Chiles oversees Florida's $57 billion pension fund. The trustees had been expected to take up tobacco-stock divestiture at a meeting this week but put off consideration of the issue indefinitely.
An advisory board last month deadlocked on divestiture and made no recommendation on the controversial proposal to the trustees.

"My sense is that the governor's people are trying to build a substantive case from his point of view," said Tom Herndon, Chiles' former chief of staff and now head of the agency overseeing Florida's pension fund.

The key vote belongs to state Treasurer Bill Nelson, an elected official who opposes smoking but who has also voiced strong sympathy for the state's fiduciarly duties to get the best investment returns. He has not spoken publicly on divestiture.
Aides to Nelson said he worries about depressed investment returns if the state jettisons its tobacco holdings. Tobacco shares bring the fund about $30 million each year.
"It's really not so much of one convincing the other," said Nelson's spokesman, Don Pride. "Bill is requesting additional analysis."

The third trustee is Comptroller Robert Milligan, who opposes divestiture and argues that the fund's tobacco holdings have outperformed other equity investments by nearly two to one over the past decade.
"I think Nelson is wrestling with it, and the governor is trying to develop some good substantive material to base a contrary view," Herndon said. "And Nelson would probably be convinced."
A spokeswoman for Chiles, Karen Pankowski, said the governor was fully aware of the trustees' fiduciary responsibililties to Florida's 725,000 state workers and retirees.
"The governor would not do anything to jeopardise the state pension fund, but he believes that investing in tobacco is becoming an increasingly risky proposition," she said.
Other state governments, too, are debating divesting tobacco stocks.

"There's debate in almost all the states where there's Medicaid litigation," said Brad Krevor of the Tobacco Control Resource Centre, an advocacy group in Boston that tracks state governments' actions on tobacco stocks.

Florida and 18 other states are suing tobacco companies to recoup the costs of treating people with smoking-related sicknesses. Florida's lawsuit claims $1 billion or more in Medicaid costs, and it is expected to go to trial on Aug. 4.
Only Maryland's pension funds have exited tobacco stocks completely, according to Krevor.

New York has frozen its tobacco holdings in some state pension funds, Texas has emptied one of its state-worker pension accounts of tobacco stock, and the large New York State Teachers Retirement Fund is shying away from tobacco equities but has stopped short of dropping them altogether, Krevor said.

The participants of one large pension fund, the non-governmental College Retirement Equities Fund, decided by an overwhelming 72 percent last fall that tobacco stocks were appropriate for their $179 billion fund.

Krevor said the tone of the debate at state governments has changed recently, with the investment risk of tobacco companies facing billions of dollars in lawsuits taking centre stage over arguments that tobacco stocks are bad social policy for government institutions.
